newsitem.title: CANADA: Heat on Bank of Canada to prop up weak dollar.
newsitem.headline: Heat on Bank of Canada to prop up weak dollar.

text.p: Canada's bleeding dollar will remain in intensive care unless the Bank of Canada intervenes to match a recent U.S. interest rate hike, economists said on Wednesday.

The Canadian dollar weakened past the key C$1.3900 (US$0.7194) level this week, setting off another round of speculation that the central bank would raise its key bank rate by 25 basis points to shore up the currency.
The central bank has not raised its key bank rate, which currently sits at a 35-year-low of 3.25 percent, since February 1995.

"What we have to see is the Bank of Canada actually signalling to markets that monetary conditions should be moving on a slightly tighter track," said Michael Gregory, economist and strategist with Lehman Brothers.
Gregory said he expected the central bank to raise rates within the next week.

A Canadian rate hike would match a similar move by the U.S. Federal Reserve. Last week, Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan raised U.S. rates 25 basis points in a pre-emptive strike amid signs of creeping U.S. inflation.

If U.S. growth continued its torrid pace, Greenspan would likely raise rates again when the Fed meets in May -- a move that could spell the end of the Bank of Canada's so-called "made-in-Canada" interest rate policy.
That policy refers to Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen's decision in 1995 to lower Canadian interest rates even while U.S. interest rates were unchanged.
"Markets clearly view last week's (U.S.) rate hike as the first in a series of Fed tightenings," said Stephen Wateridge, managing director of corporate foreign exchange for CIBC Wood Gundy.
The widening of the spread between Canadian and U.S. interest rates to 225 basis points has already triggered a stampede of Canada-dollar selling in overseas markets.
The Canadian dollar has lost more than 3.0 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar in the past two months.
Only domestic corporate buying of Canada dollars and some recent interest by Canadian exporters to hold the Canadian currency had stemmed a further collapse of the currency, Wateridge said.
The steady erosion of the dollar flies in the face of Canada's relatively strong economic fundamentals, which had been expected to help underpin the currency in a crisis.

Canada's economy was expected to grow more than 3.0 percent in 1997, while inflation should remain within the central bank's target range of 1.0-3.0 percent, according to a Reuters poll of economists.
But jittery equity markets and controversy surrounding junior mining company Bre-X Minerals Ltd have added to the interest rate pressure on the dollar.
Speculation that Bre-X's Indonesian gold mine may contain much less gold than previously reported has set off a selling frenzy in mining stocks on the Toronto Stock Exchange.
Thiessen, however, appears unfazed by the bellowing for a quick interest rate strike.
The Bank of Canada has more room to maneuver now than it did before, but that should not be interpreted as a pledge not to raise interest rates, Thiessen recently told reporters.
